articles.title: Why a US-Russia showdown left Morocco celebrating
articles.summary: An impasse between the US and Russia at the UN means its peacekeeping mission in Western Sahara has ended after 35 years.
body: Morocco claims Western Sahara as part of its territory

Morocco has welcomed the end of a decades-long UN peacekeeping mission in Western Sahara, after a diplomatic showdown between the US and Russia left the Security Council unable to agree on its future.

The council failed on Friday to renew the mandate of the UN Mission for the Referendum in Western Sahara (Minurso) after Russia vetoed a US-backed proposal. A rival Russian draft to extend the mission also failed to secure enough votes.

The decision raises questions about the future of Africa's longest territorial dispute and the fragile ceasefire between Morocco, which claims Western Sahara, and the Polisario Front which has been fighting for the territory's independence for more than 50 years.
Western Sahara, on Africa's north-west coast, was a Spanish colony until 1975. It has significant phosphate reserves and valuable fishing grounds along its Atlantic coast.
As Spain prepared to withdraw, both Morocco and Mauritania claimed the territory.
The International Court of Justice found historical ties of allegiance but no territorial sovereignty that overrode the Sahrawi people's right to self-determination.

Morocco's then King Hassan II responded by organising the Green March. On 6 November 1975 about 350,000 Moroccan civilians entered the territory in a mass demonstration intended to put pressure on Spain.

Days later, Spain signed the Madrid Accords with Morocco and Mauritania, agreeing to transfer administrative control. Morocco took the northern two-thirds and Mauritania the southern third. The agreement did not settle the question of sovereignty.
The Polisario Front, an independence movement founded in 1973, opposed the deal. It saw it as replacing Spanish colonial rule with Moroccan and Mauritanian control.
Mauritania renounced its claim in 1979, but Morocco continued fighting Polisario.
Algeria became Polisario main regional ally, providing military support and hosting its leadership and thousands of Sahrawi refugees in camps near the city of Tindouf.
The North African country says its position is based on the right to self-determination, while Morocco sees Western Sahara as an integral part of its territory.

Morocco and Algeria fought a brief border war in 1963 over disagreements about territory inherited from French colonial rule. Their relationship has remained tense, with Western Sahara at the centre of their dispute.
After 16 years of fighting, Morocco and Polisario agreed to a UN-brokered ceasefire in 1991, with the territory divided by a sand wall, or berm, to keep the rival forces apart.
The UN established Minurso to monitor the ceasefire and organise a referendum on the territory's future. Sahrawis were meant to choose between independence and integration with Morocco.
The vote was scheduled for 1992 but never took place. The two sides could not agree on who would be eligible to participate, with disputes over voter identification becoming a major obstacle.
In 2007, Morocco put forward a proposal for autonomy, which would see Sahrawis managing their internal affairs, while Rabat retained control over defence and foreign relations.
Thousands of Moroccans marched into Western Sahara in 1975 in what became known as the Green March
The Polisario Front and Algeria rejected the plan, insisting on a referendum that included independence as an option.
Years of UN-sponsored negotiations failed to produce a breakthrough.
The ceasefire broke down in November 2020, when Polisario said it was resuming armed struggle.

But following a long diplomatic campaign by Morocco, the UN Security Council voted in 2025 in favour of a resolution backing the autonomy plan as the "most feasible" solution for the disputed territory.
While most Sahrawis live in the part of Western Sahara controlled by Morocco, tens of thousands are estimated to be in refugee camps in Algeria.
The US proposed extending Minurso's mandate for another year, but its draft went beyond the usual renewal.
It would have removed the word "referendum" from the mission's name and made Morocco's autonomy proposal the sole basis for further negotiations.
The draft received the support of 11 of the Security Council's 15 members, including France and the UK but Russia vetoed it, arguing that it was too favourable to Morocco.
Russia then proposed extending Minurso's mandate without changing its terms. That draft also failed, receiving only two votes in favour.

Minurso's mandate expired at the end of Saturday, 31 October. The UN said the following day that the mission had entered a liquidation period, with a reduced team overseeing the transfer of military equipment and other assets.
The UN mission has been in Western Sahara since 1991
UN Secretary-General António Guterres said the Sahrawi people's right to self-determination must be respected and warned of the risk of renewed hostilities.

The Polisario Front condemned the US proposal. Its representative, Sidi Omar, thanked Russia for vetoing it, saying it would "torpedo the foundations of the UN peace process" and threaten regional and international peace.
Morocco, meanwhile, said the mission's personnel and equipment should leave the territory in the coming days, arguing that Western Sahara issue should no longer be considered by the Security Council.
Minurso had 155 military personnel and was expected to cost $62m (£46m) in the financial year beginning in June, according to a UN report.
Morocco's royal palace welcomed the failure to renew Minurso's mandate.
In Laayoune, the territory's largest city, footage showed people celebrating, waving Moroccan flags and displaying portraits of King Mohammed VI.

"The decision is an opportunity for Rabat to challenge what it sees as an international mechanism that has failed to resolve the dispute," Issam Laaroussi, a Moroccan expert in international relations, tells the BBC.
He said Morocco would now have more room to push its autonomy proposal and shift negotiations away from a referendum on independence towards autonomy under Moroccan sovereignty.
The decision does not, however, change Western Sahara's legal status or amount to international recognition of Moroccan sovereignty.
Western Sahara remains on the UN list of non-self-governing territories, while the African Union officially recognises its independence, as the Sahrawi Arab Democratic Republic (SADR).
But the decision comes after several countries backed the position of Morocco, which in recent years has made securing international support for its claim a central part of its foreign policy.
In 2020, the US recognised Moroccan sovereignty over Western Sahara as part of an agreement to establish diplomatic relations between Morocco and Israel.
France also backed Morocco's autonomy plan as the basis for resolving the dispute in 2024.
Thousands of Sahrawis live in refugee camps in Algeria
Morocco rejoined the African Union in 2017, more than three decades after leaving its predecessor, the Organisation of African Unity, in protest at the SADR's admission.
Since returning, Rabat has sought to build support for its position from within the organisation. At least 10 African countries have opened diplomatic missions in the territory in support of Rabat.
"Morocco is not necessarily seeking to abandon the UN process, but to change the framework for negotiations and draw greater support from regional organisations," says Laaroussi.
Addressing a special joint session of parliament on Monday, House of Representatives Speaker Ahmed Touizi hailed the end of Minurso as a victory for the country's diplomacy.
He said the country should now move from "managing the dispute to implementing its autonomy plan under Moroccan sovereignty, while pressing ahead with development projects in the territory."
The fear is that Minurso's departure could lead to renewed fighting.
The mission has monitored military developments and helped reduce the risk of escalation.
Aid organisation Oxfam warned that losing its monitoring and de-escalation role could undermine stability, with serious consequences for civilians.
Laaroussi admits that the mission's departure could create security gaps.
"Minurso's departure does not create the original conflict, because the conflict is already there, but it could aggravate an already fragile security environment," he says.
The UN decision has also fuelled nationalist rhetoric online.
Several Moroccan users have shared AI-generated images of themselves in military uniform, declaring their readiness to fight for Morocco's sovereignty over Western Sahara.

In Morocco, Western Sahara is widely regarded as a national cause. Political parties that are often divided on other issues are united in supporting the country's claim to sovereignty over the territory.
Foreign Minister Nasser Bourita has said the end of the mission does not mean the end of the ceasefire, and that Rabat remains committed to it "within respect of its security and sovereignty."
Polisario has not said what it will do next.
Any resumption of fighting could well draw in Algeria, as tensions with Morocco remain high.

articles.title: Indonesia's toxic haze is giving its neighbours a political headache
articles.summary: Governments in Singapore and Malaysia are split between anxious citizens and an irascible neighbour.
body: The haze stemming from wildfires in Indonesia has drifted into Singapore and Malaysia
The haze billowing out from wildfires in the Indonesian regions of Kalimantan, Papua and Sumatra knows no borders.
Carried by winds to nearby Singapore and Malaysia, the toxic smog has in recent weeks impacted populations across maritime South East Asia, triggering respiratory illnesses and headaches.
It's also giving the region's governments a different kind of headache - split between the mounting frustrations of their citizens and the risk of souring diplomatic ties with Indonesia.

"People are fed up, angry and anxious," Eugene Tan, associate professor of law at the Singapore Management University, tells the BBC. "The governments have to respond to them, or else what is more an external issue has become an internal one with ample headroom for politicisation."
Indonesia's wildfires are a yearly occurrence, widely associated with industrial-scale land clearing to make way for crops like oil palm.
But the blazes this year have been particularly difficult to tame due to a strong El Niño, which has exacerbated drought conditions in the country's forests and peatlands.
Whereas previous haze episodes in Singapore and Malaysia have typically lasted for a few days, this time it stretched into weeks.

In Malaysia, locals started a boycott of Indonesian products in protest against the haze, after lawmaker Syed Saddiq called for sanctions on companies linked to the wildfires and said Malaysians should "treat them as an outcast in the region".
There have also been complaints in Singapore, a country that has come to expect seamless efficiency from its leaders.

"There appears to be the view that the government dropped the ball in dealing with the haze, given that it was known that the El Niño weather phenomenon would be severe and that early warning was given," says Tan.
"Clearly, Singaporeans expect the government to decisively deal with the polluters."
Singapore's government, for its part, has made it clear that the haze problem is a priority.
Hundreds of haze shelters have been set up across the island, and masks are being distributed to children, the elderly and other vulnerable residents.
Authorities have also said they're looking to strengthen existing haze legislation and are investigating 10 Singapore-registered companies for potential links to the wildfires in Indonesia.

Last week, Singapore's foreign minister Vivian Balakrishnan met Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto in Jakarta for what the former described as "honest" and "sincere" conversations that produced "constructive approaches".
The meeting came as both countries announced they would set up a joint task force to deal with the haze - an apparent détente after weeks of simmering bilateral tensions.
Singapore's foreign minister Vivian Balakrishnan met President Prabowo in Jakarta on Wednesday
As the haze spiralled into yet another crisis for Prabowo's beleaguered administration, some officials pushed back against criticism.
One senior official ruffled feathers when he said the wildfires were out of human control and that oxygen in neighbouring Singapore and Malaysia "also comes from our forests".
That remark was "disappointing" and "not right", according to Singaporean senior minister K Shanmugam - a rare rebuke from the city state, which prides itself on its diplomatic prowess.

"The haze is affecting our health seriously, and it's really unacceptable," Shanmugam told reporters. Since the haze impacts citizens on both sides of the border, there should not be "any bilateral issues" in addressing it, he added.
"The Indonesian public is suffering as well, and it is in Indonesia's interest as much as ours to deal with the companies that are causing these problems."
Days later, Indonesia announced it would reduce gas exports to Singapore, citing domestic energy needs - a move that many saw as retaliation to Singapore's rhetoric.

To be sure, Indonesia has faced recent electricity shortages in parts of the country. Singapore also says the reduction, which amounts to less than 2% of its total daily demand, will have little impact on its gas supply.

But the abrupt announcement came just days after Indonesia's energy minister warned that they could halt gas exports to countries that don't "respect Indonesia". That same day, Prabowo made reference to "countries that like to insult Indonesia" when talking about the wildfires.

"It's a tired playbook of using Singapore as the bogeyman, driven by the 'abang-adik' [big brother-little brother] syndrome," Tan says, referring to a historical dynamic that Singapore's leaders have long tried to shrug off: the expectation that it should defer to its larger neighbours.
"Singapore leaders expressing concerns about the haze and how it affects the people of both countries have been taken to mean that Singapore has been disrespectful to its neighbour."
Schools were closed in parts of Malaysia when haze reached unhealthy levels this month
In contrast, Malaysia's official rhetoric on the haze has been relatively muted.
Its foreign minister Mohamad Hasan has ruled out lodging a formal diplomatic protest with Indonesia or taking legal action, saying such actions "would mean we were prepared to sever relations".
For now, Malaysia has agreed to explore a memorandum of understanding with Indonesia to strengthen wildfire prevention efforts.
It would also rely on diplomatic mechanisms, Mohamad said - like the Asean Agreement on Transboundary Haze Pollution.
The agreement, which came into effect in 2003, commits members of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean) to collaborate on tackling the recurring haze.
But many see it as toothless, as it is unable to punish agricultural companies linked to wildfires or to force individual governments to do so.
The agreement has turned out to be "just not worth the paper it was signed on", says James Chin, professor of Asian studies at the University of Tasmania.
"The moment the haze disappears, the moment the political pressure's off, it's back to business as usual."
In 2016, Asean countries had set a goal to eliminate haze in the region by 2020. When that deadline drifted quietly by, they set a new target of achieving the goal by 2030 instead.

Complicating Malaysia's position is the fact that it is also a major palm oil producer. The commodity is often linked to commercial "slash-and-burn" practices that are widely blamed for the region's wildfires.
Malaysia has at times dealt with acute haze stemming from blazes on local land.

In 2019, when Malaysia pointed to hotspots in Indonesia's peatlands as the cause of the haze shrouding the region, Indonesian authorities pointed the finger back at Malaysia, claiming the smog came from their side.
"As long as we place a lot of importance on oil palm planting, [the haze] is going to recur," says Ei Sun Oh, principal adviser at the Pacific Research Centre of Malaysia.

And even if Malaysia were to speak up, Oh adds, it's unlikely to wield the same "leverage" over Indonesia as Singapore, which is Indonesia's largest foreign investor and an offshore financial hub for many wealthy Indonesians.
For now, Malaysia "doesn't want to unduly provoke Indonesia", says Oh.
"The government is just wringing their hands till the wind blows [the problem] over. Because eventually it will blow over."

articles.title: Democrats have high hopes for midterms - but are the polls right?
articles.summary: Polls have been predicting a Democratic surge, but last-minute deciders and sampling issues mean there's no guarantee.
body: The Democratic Party has high expectations as it heads into these pivotal US midterm elections.
A historically unpopular Republican president, an American public unhappy with the rising costs of food and bills, and months of favourable polls point to a good night for them on Tuesday.

Democratic candidates lead in well over the 218 seats needed to flip control of the lower chamber of Congress, the House of Representatives, the polls suggest. And they are tied or narrowly ahead in the key Senate races.

A recent New York Times poll had the Senate race in South Carolina, a state Donald Trump won by 18 percentage points in 2024, as a tie. Recent CNN surveys put the Democrats ahead in Texas, Kansas and Maine.

Recent US political history is littered with examples where public opinion polls, even ones just days before an election, were off the mark. Trump outperformed predictions on his way to White House victories in 2016 and 2024. His narrow defeat in 2020 came after most surveys indicated a more comfortable win for Democrat Joe Biden.

Earlier this year, polls suggested Democrat Abdul El-Sayed was poised for a double-digit win in Michigan's Democratic Senate primary. Instead it was 1%. In Wisconsin's Democratic primary for governor, the candidate that had a polling lead that approached 20 points lost by a fraction of a percent.
Democrats have an identity crisis - it won't be an easy fix

According to Clifford Young, president of Ipsos Public Affairs, which conducts political and market research surveys, polling has become difficult in recent years because it's harder to reach Americans as they abandon their land lines and screen their calls. And many of those who pollsters do contact have become less willing to participate.
"Conservatives, especially those on the far right, are much more anti-establishment by nature," Young says. "And they don't participate in anything. They hate the system. That's the challenge."

If Republican voters are being undercounted in a systematic way, and polling companies don't take that into consideration when constructing their voting models, it could skew their data towards the Democrats.
That's one of the reasons why it has become trickier for pollsters to predict what the electorate will look like.
GUIDE: What are the US midterms?
IN DEPTH: The real reasons there are so few young US politicians
EXPLORE: Where the US midterms will be won and lost
VERIFY: How the US economy is really doing under Trump
NEWSLETTER: Sign up for Anthony Zurcher's analysis in your inbox
One explanation for why Trump overperformed in previous presidential elections is that his supporters – many of whom were not regular voters – flocked to the polls in higher-than-expected numbers.
That unpredictability is one of the main contributing factors to those notable recent polling misses, even if the margins in most reputable polls were only off by a few percentage points.
In a close race, those few points can make the difference between victory and defeat for a candidate. And this year, many of the key Senate races are within those narrow margins.
What's at stake for Trump in the US midterms?
In recent years, midterm general election polls have proven to be more accurate, in part because Trump - and his unique ability to draw disaffected Americans to the polls - was not on the ballot.
In 2022, they suggested Democrats would defy conventional expectations and avoid an electoral wipe-out despite Biden's low approval numbers.
While the party lost control of the House of Representatives, the margins were slim and Democrats maintained control of the US Senate.

While this year's primary results did provide bigger surprises, Young says that nominating contests have historically been volatile, with voters more likely to make up their minds at the last minute. It shouldn't be seen as an indication that the current crop of general election polls are off the mark.
It's common for the party of the president to have a bad night in the midterms.
One of the most notable examples in recent years came in 2010 when Republicans flipped more than 60 House seats and made gains in the Senate.

It came off the back of an economy struggling to recover from the financial crash and conservative fears over President Barack Obama's healthcare reforms. A defeat had been predicted by the polls but not quite on that scale.

The roles are reversed this time, with the Democrats in opposition and the economy on the minds of voters. But there are a number of reasons why Democrats may not have as good a night as history might suggest or as some might expect, given Trump's low approval rating.
Firstly, much of the territory in play in this election Trump conquered with ease in the presidential election just two years ago. It's like a home game for Republicans.
Then there have been changes to House election boundaries over the years that have meant fewer seats switch between parties.
Thirdly, there are fewer swing voters due to the deeper polarisation of the country. Some experts describe the electorate as calcified.
There's also the cash advantage Republicans have enjoyed which has given them hundreds of millions of dollars to spend on attack ads in the final weeks.
Obama gives a press conference the day after the heavy 2010 midterms defeat
Polling models try to capture shifting fundamentals. And a well-designed poll is built to anticipate issues that may make it less than reliable.

Individual polls do have a built-in margin of error – a statistical level of uncertainty based on the sampling size compared to the population as a whole. Taken as an aggregate, polling averages and not individual surveys can provide a more accurate prediction.

At the moment, even the kind of polling lean we saw in recent presidential elections would suggest Democrats are likely to have a good night on 3 November. And polling inaccuracies can go both ways. In last year's state and special elections, Democrats outperformed most surveys as it was their voters who turned out in unexpectedly larger numbers.

The sight of Trump holding rallies in the final days of the campaign in states he won comfortably in 2024 will have lifted Democrats' hopes that Republican internal polling has conservative candidates in trouble.
Voter voices: What issues matter most to Americans?
There's always the chance that voters change their minds right up until election day, however.

Sometimes there are late shifts that can alter the dynamics of a race. Sometimes undecided voters, which still account for a key segment of the electorate in many of these races, all break the same way.
In polling, there will always be some level of uncertainty – and managing that is the art that goes along with the science.
"I think we're doing a better job," says Young. "But part of the problem we always have is not just with the pollsters. Part of it is that we're dealing with humans. Humans are not easy."

articles.title: Musk pumps $446m into US midterms, as campaign spending set to 'shatter' records
articles.summary: The 2026 campaign is projected to cost nearly $12bn - BBC Verify looks into where all that money has come from.
body: The US midterms campaign is set to be the most expensive on record - with the total cost projected to reach nearly $12bn (£9bn), according to Open Secrets, an independent organisation that tracks campaign finance.

Most of the spending is driven by outside political groups - known as Super Political Action Committees (Super Pacs) - pouring large sums of money into some key races ahead of election day on 3 November.
The top individual donor is billionaire businessman Elon Musk, who has spent almost half a billion dollars backing Republican candidates, particularly in Texas where many of his companies are based.
BBC Verify has looked into the figures and where the money was spent.
There are rules on how much people, parties and political action committees (Pacs) can give directly to candidates.

But Super Pacs can accept unlimited contributions from individuals, corporations, labour unions, and other political committees. They can't give that money directly to candidates but they can spend it supporting them indirectly.
According to the latest Federal Election Commission, external (FEC) filings which run to mid-October, more than $9.5bn had been spent in this midterms cycle.
Pacs and Super Pacs make up more than half of that - at about $5.5bn - with their spending in the last couple of months almost doubling.
Candidates, parties and outside groups have to report their spending to the FEC, but the full totals won't be available until after the midterm elections.
However, Open Secrets has projected the total will be $11.9bn based on trends in past cycles.
This would be about 30% more than what was spent during the last midterm elections in 2022.
The top 40 donors gave $2.4bn up until 14 October, according to the liberal-leaning think tank Brennan Center for Justice, external, which is a record high for that point in a midterms cycle.
"Spending in the 2026 midterms is shattering records, with more of the money coming from the wealthiest donors and groups this election," says Michael Beckel, a US campaign finance expert.

As well as individuals, organisations can also give to Pacs. For example, Geosor Corp and Fund for Policy Reform, both founded by the billionaire financier George Soros, have given a combined $102m to liberal groups.
Aside from Soros, former New York City mayor and businessman Michael Bloomberg has been the biggest Democratic donor, giving more than $60m.

Several billionaires including Jeff Yass, who runs one of the world's largest trading firms, and Richard and Elizabeth Uihlein, the owners of a US business supply company, have given over $100m this campaign to Republican causes, according to FEC filings.
But Musk has given by far the most of any individual, donating almost half a billion dollars as of October.
Musk has given most of this to a Super Pac he set up in 2024 called America PAC, as well as to the Republican-aligned Senate Leadership Fund.
Most of his money has been spent on the Texas Senate race, supporting Republican candidate Ken Paxton, who is running against Democratic candidate James Talarico.
Elon Musk worked for the Trump administration last year and has attended events at the White House since
Three takeaways from Elon Musk's latest political donations
America PAC's investments in the Texas race total more than $45m. It has also invested around $10m into both of the Senate races in Michigan and Ohio.

"Crypto companies have also been very active this cycle, with Ripple and Coinbase combining to give $63 million to fund Super Pacs promoting the crypto industry's interests," says Brendan J Glavin of Open Secrets.

Campaigns and political groups spend money trying to reach voters in a variety of ways - including hiring staff to do on-the-ground voter outreach and hosting campaign events like rallies. They also spend money to conduct internal polling.
However, the majority of funds are spent on advertising - especially on TV.
In this cycle, $11.15bn has been spent on advertising up until the end of October, according to ad tracking firm AdImpact, external.
"Traditional broadcast television remains the top beneficiary of advertising expenditures, though expenditures on digital ads continue to increase," says Beckel.
Similarly to Musk's spending, AdImpact tracked that most of the money has been spent on advertising in the Senate races in Michigan, Texas and Ohio, followed by Iowa and Maine.

articles.title: US strikes Iran’s Qeshm Island as Vance voices optimism about a deal
articles.summary: Strikes on eve of US midterms reportedly target surface-to-air missiles being used against US assets
body: The ⁠US launched limited strikes on ​Iran’s Qeshm Island late on Monday, hours after the vice-president, JD Vance, said he was optimistic that diplomatic efforts to end the war were moving in the right direction.

The strikes, first reported by the Wall Street Journal, came on the eve of crucial midterm elections in which Donald Trump’s Republican party is expected to be punished by voters for the cascading effect the war has had on the cost of living.
Unnamed US officials cited by the WSJ and other outlets described the attacks as defensive in nature.
Trump was asked earlier on Monday whether he had considered resuming strikes on Iran after Tuesday’s midterm elections and replied “no”.
Related: Oil price falls amid hope of a breakthrough to end Iran war
Several explosions were ⁠heard ⁠on Qeshm ​Island on Monday evening, according to Iranian state media, with local outlets describing their cause as unclear.
The strikes targeted surface-to-air missiles being used against US assets, according to Reuters and the Associated Press.

US Central ‌Command did ​not immediately ⁠respond to ​a request for ​comment from the Reuters news agency, but the WSJ described the attacks as part of a series of strikes carried out against the country in recent weeks that had not been made public.

The paper reported that the recent strikes had been carried out on a smaller scale and purposefully kept secret by the Trump administration so as not to signal ‌any intent of resuming the military campaign against Iran.

The US has targeted Qeshm Island on multiple occasions throughout the war. Positioned in the mouth of the strait of Hormuz, the island has been used in the past to launch attacks on shipping in the waterway.

Despite attacks having ceased in recent weeks, Iran has continued to enforce its closure of the strait by targeting oil tankers, shipping containers and other vessels attempting to transit the waterway.
On Monday, Vance said he and Trump were optimistic about securing a deal with Iran, after Tehran revealed indirect negotiations with Washington.

“The president and I both feel pretty good about the prospects for potentially coming to a negotiated settlement,” Vance told reporters. “We’ve certainly made some progress. We’ll see if we can make some more.”
Speaking to Fox News hours before the polls opened in the US on Tuesday, Trump continued to play down the significance of the conflict and its effects on the US economy.
“There’s no war raging. It could happen if they don’t make a deal, but they want to make a deal very badly and there’s a very good chance we make a deal.”

However, he said the US might still “have to go after Pickaxe Mountain” – referring to a fortified underground site in central Iran that is suspected to be a nuclear facility – but said it would not be a “big deal” and could be done in “one hour”.

Speaking from Washington in his closing message of the midterms campaign, Trump hailed a sharp drop in oil prices as his administration touted renewed diplomatic efforts being made to end the war. Rising petrol prices have caused by the war have become a signature issue of the midterm elections.

articles.title: Tuesday briefing: Britain is moving the goalposts for its migrant workers
articles.summary: In today’s newsletter: Shabana Mahmood has softened rules for care workers after an outcry, but thousands of other migrant workers face an uncertain future
body: Good morning. “Settlement should not be automatic, it should be earned,” home secretary Shabana Mahmood told the Commons yesterday as she unveiled a radical shake-up of the rules governing how long foreign workers and refugees have to wait before they are granted the right to live in the UK indefinitely.

What Mahmood insisted was a “fair solution” that would cut welfare spending by billions had been characterised as the first serious test of whether Andy Burnham could keep the left of the Labour party in line, after the original plans were met with outrage from backbenchers, migrants rights groups and unions.

In the event she avoided outright revolt, but was accused of watering down more punitive proposals to appease her party critics, while charities are furious at stringent new requirements for refugees, and legal experts warned retrospective rule changes now faced by many migrant workers undermine the rule of law.

In an endeavour to sift the substance from the spin, I spoke to home affairs editor, Rajeev Syal, about the detail of the plans and community affairs correspondent, Chris Osuh, about the people whose lives they will change.

Commonwealth summit | Andy Burnham will ask countries affected by Britain’s role in slavery to help shape an expected formal apology, Downing Street has indicated, arguing that their input is indispensable in crafting an enduring message.

Defence | British troops and their European allies would be allowed to fire back if attacked by Russians when potentially stationed as peacekeepers in Ukraine after a ceasefire, western officials said.

Iran | The ⁠US launched limited strikes on ​Iran’s Qeshm Island late on Monday, ⁠according to reports in US media, hours after US vice-president JD Vance said he was optimistic diplomatic efforts to end the war were moving in the right direction.

Sweden | Supermarket chains in at least seven European countries have said the temperatures of refrigerators and freezers in some of their shops soared overnight to as high as 50C, echoing a cyber-attack last month that caused millions of euros of damage in France.

US midterms | Donald Trump unveiled the delayed results of his $14m renovation of Washington DC’s Lincoln Memorial reflecting pool in what is expected to be his final press conference before voters head to the polls for the midterm elections.

The home secretary wanted to double the wait for settlement, also known as indefinite leave to remain (ILR), to 10 years for new arrivals, as well as retrospectively for those who came in the post-Brexit wave. Some lower-paid migrants, including care workers, would have to wait 15 years.
The proposals caused controversy. Unions described the plans for retrospective changes for much-needed care workers as “cruel and unconscionable”.

A year later the political context is very different. Andy Burnham has succeeded Starmer, and the threat posed to Labour by Reform has receded significantly, while net migration is plummeting. But migration remains a top concern for voters, and YouGov polling released yesterday found that nearly half of Britons support extending the waiting period for legal migrants before they are granted ILR.

Meantime, the criticism of Mahmood’s plans has only become more vocal. In June, while still on the backbenches before her promotion back to cabinet, Angela Rayner said the care worker proposal was “un-British”. In September, the energy secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, said the plans would have been “tough” for her family, who came to Britain as refugees.
And last weekend, the Guardian reported on a letter signed by parliamentarians alongside campaigners and health professionals describing the proposals as “an iteration of Windrush era policies”.

Ahead of the statement, there were reports of up to 100 Labour MPs ready to rebel if Mahmood didn’t soften her original proposals – though quite how is unclear, because she doesn’t require a vote on primary legislation to put through these changes.

In the event, no rebellion was necessary. While Mahmood has tightened the rules on ILR significantly, doubling the standard wait to qualify to 10 years, she scrapped her planned 15 year wait for lower-paid workers.

As Rajeev sets out in this helpful explainer, under pressure from health unions, the home secretary offered a carve-out for care workers, allowing an estimated 280,000 and their dependents to apply for ILR after five years.

Faster routes will be available for highest band taxpayers, for example, and some public service workers including doctors, nurses and teachers. But, as Rajeev points out, thousands of lower-paid workers will still face the shock of having to wait a decade before being able to apply to settle in the UK, despite being told when they first arrived the wait was five years. The changes will mean half a million people face longer waits for settled status.

“The new rules also place particularly stringent requirements for settlement on refugees,” Rajeev tells me – with those entering via small boat set to wait up to 30 years for permanent settlement and those claiming asylum having entered the country legally waiting a decade. The Refugee Council condemned the plans as “unfair and unworkable” and likely to harm refugee integration. The Law Society went further, suggesting the new rules contravene the Refugee Convention.
The exception will be the small number of refugees who enter through designated safe and legal routes like the scheme for Afghan women and girls and Palestinians.

Both Zack Polanski and Kemi Badenoch, politicians at either end of the political spectrum, have dismissed care work as “wiping bottoms” in recent years. There’s a crude assumption that, because it is poorly paid, it must demand minimal effort. But I know from my own family’s experience of social care about the patience, skill and humanity involved in this kind of work.

It was the prospect of even more overwhelming uncertainty that people found so crushing, Chris Osuh tells me. He has been interviewing care workers around Manchester about their professional conditions since the changes were first mooted: “When somebody’s waiting for settlement, the uncertainty never goes away”. And the practical reality is that during this waiting period individuals are still paying out visa costs on top of taxes, while their career ambitions and earning capacity may be limited because some jobs are contingent on having secured ILR. “Basically it makes your life a lot more precarious for longer.”

It’s worth reiterating that these changes affect people who’ve arrived legally in the UK through pathways intended to help British people. “You’re doing vital, hard, underpaid work where there are huge skill shortages”, he says. It’s also the case that some care workers find themselves tied to exploitative employers by strict visa arrangements, something Mahmood acknowledged yesterday when she introduced safety nets for those exploited by “rogue sponsors”.

Data suggests 19% of the care workforce are non-EU citizens, and many come from places such as Nigeria, Ghana and broader sub-Saharan Africa. As the prime minister opens dialogue around apology for Britain’s role in the transatlantic slave trade, it’s hard not to see this as “a continuation of an exploitative relationship”, adds Chris. “Once again, Britain looks to all those countries that it once colonised to replace the labour that was lost during Brexit”.

Even before Mahmood stood up to make her statement, Chris Philp, the shadow home secretary, was accusing her of surrendering to “the open-borders Labour left” while Nigel Farage, whose Reform UK party wants to get rid of ILR completely, claimed she was “losing the fight with the far left”.

Unions representing care workers welcomed the concessions yesterday evening, while care sector bosses expressed relief that they weren’t about to lose a whole tranche of their workforce. But Rajeev cautions against reading these compromises purely as capitulation to Unison, one of Labour’s biggest financial backers, or to avoid cabinet rancour.

“If you look at the plans as a whole,” he tells me, “aside from the compromise around care workers, this still amounts to a radical hardening of policy that she has pushed through. And Andy Burnham supports it because he wants to win back the ‘red wall’.”

“This is about fairness in a system that Burnham’s already expressed a very personal interest in,” says Rajeev. Burnham has repeatedly praised the dedication of care home staff who looked after his father, Roy, before his death in September. But Burnham has also reiterated that his version of fairness is one that passes the Makerfield test.

As our political editor Pippa Crerar puts it in this analysis, the prime minister regards migration as a means to show people who’ve lost faith in politics that the government is prepared to listen and act. The next challenge for Mahmood is to convince the public of exactly that.

Democratic congresswoman Haley Stevens has endorsed the Republican candidate for the Senate after a spat with her party’s own candidate in Michigan, Abdul El-Sayed. Bill Drysdale saw the Porsche 904 at Silverstone racetrack when he was 26. He instantly fell in love but realised that buying the car was unlikely, due to its over £1mil price tag. Still, he promised himself that one day he would have it.

That was 61 years ago – today, 87-year-old Drysdale has the car of his dreams, just without the hefty price tag. He decided to build the car from scratch after retiring as an engineer at 60. It took him eight years to complete what he has dubbed the “Porsche 904FF”; the double Fs meaning “effing fake”. Drysdale has always had a passion for cars. articles.title: ‘Our aim is that children are protected’: besieged West Bank school fortifies its defences against settler violence
articles.summary: After deaths of five students at hands of Israeli settlers in last academic year, al-Mughayyir’s teachers and pupils are on high alert
body: This year, parents in al-Mughayyir had to be persuaded to send their children back to school. Israeli settlers had killed five teenage students last academic year – one of them at the school gates.

To reassure parents, teachers of the public secondary school gave a tour of the facilities, which they had spent the summer break fortifying. Metal fences now towered over the schoolyard’s walls and the door had been replaced by a sturdy metal gate. A new wall shielded the classrooms from a hilltop where last academic year a settler had shot dead two people, including a student.

Al-Mughayyir, a town of about 3,000 people north-east of Ramallah in the occupied West Bank, is under a siege by Israeli settlers. Armed settlers regularly raid the village, assaulting residents, attacking homes and seizing livestock. Israeli soldiers set up checkpoints that prevent people from entering or leaving for hours at a time.
The school is isolated on the very edge of the village, close to its entrance. Settlers stage their raids around the school, attacking under the watchful eye of the Israeli military.

A single Israeli soldier stands at the entrance of the village, his rifle slung over his shoulder as he paces back and forth idly. It is he who decides who can come and go in the village. The excited shouting of schoolchildren playing can be heard from where he stands; the children’s voices echo across the otherwise quiet village, most shops shuttered despite it being a weekday.

Residents say the violence is part of a wider project to displace Palestinians from their land, one that has already driven smaller communities from their homes. Now, they fear the same tactics are being turned against an entire village in an attempt to make life so intolerable that residents leave.

“When the settlers began their attacks, they began in the Jordan valley area, displacing communities of farmers consisting of 10, 20 people. Now, they are trying to displace entire villages. What’s happening in al-Mughayyir is the beginning of this project,” said Ameen Abu Alia, the 54-year-old mayor of the town.

Abu Alia has watched as the number of settler outposts – small groups of Israeli shepherds who establish outposts near Palestinian communities – has multiplied around the town over the last three years. In 2023, there was just one settler outpost near the town. Now, there are 12.

Settlers now enter the town on a regular basis, shutting down roads, and harassing residents as they graze their sheep on fields next to the school and deeper in the village. Residents say that settlers steal sheep from villagers, provoking fights with residents who depend on livestock for their livelihood. When villagers resist they can be arrested, or killed.

In 2024, settlers attacked a home in al-Mughayyir. Waheed Abu Naim, a 37-year-old schoolteacher, rushed to help defend it, trying to push the settler away. The settler put a pistol to Abu Naim’s breast and squeezed the trigger. Abu Naim closed his eyes, but no explosion followed – the settler had already fired his last bullet.

The settler siege is a tactic seen in the West Bank before. Small settler outposts run by teenagers and a few adults have popped up around small Bedouin communities in the Jordan river valley since 2023 and engaged in a steadily escalating campaign of violence to make life intolerable for the Palestinians living there. In Ras ‘Ein al-‘Auja in the south Jordan valley, settlers drove out the last inhabitants of the community in January after they could no longer endure the constant attacks, in a pattern similar to what is now happening in al-Mughayyir.

Despite settlements being considered illegal under international law, the Israeli government has taken few steps to curtail steadily expanding settler violence, beyond issuing a few condemnations. Extremist ministers in the Netanyahu government have equipped settlers with guns and vehicles and the rate of settlement expansion has soared under the current government.

The settler outposts are not visible from al-Mughayyir but are present just beyond the arid hills that ring the village. Residents drive fast along the winding 1-mile road that leads into the town, wary of how exposed they are to settler attacks along the way.

Local people describe close cooperation between Israeli soldiers and settlers. They often see them talking as settlers enter the town, and soldiers provide protection for settlers, only intervening when they – not Palestinians – are under threat.
In early September two teenagers, Omar al-Nassan, 19, and Khalil Abu Alia, 16, were killed by settlers and Israeli soldiers as the pair tried to stop settlers from taking their sheep, Abu Alia said.

“The last theft was of 60 sheep in the centre of the village. Ten military vehicles came. They came into the centre of the village and laid siege to that area. They stole the sheep and opened fire on people,” said Abu Alia.

The Israeli military said that it entered the village to provide security for an Israeli civilian and police trying to retrieve livestock, and that it fired on “key instigators” when Palestinians threw stones at the soldiers.

The village’s olive groves remain unpicked, despite the arrival of the season’s first rains, which signal the fruit is ripe: villagers are wary of the settler violence they have seen accompany harvests in neighbouring villages. Settlers have carried out more than 170 attacks since the start of the harvest at the end of September, according to Yesh Din, an Israeli rights group.

While settlers attack residents, the Israeli military is placing increasing restrictions on villagers. Olive production is a key industry, but residents have been prohibited from harvesting without prior military approval. The military closes the only entry to the village for several hours a day, several times a week, preventing people from going to work and teachers from reaching the school.
The result has been a slow strangulation of people’s livelihoods. Already, three families have left the village to be closer to their work, fearful of the constant road closures.
“Someone who has no money is now forced to sell part of their flock, and end their involvement in farming and search for other work,” said Abu Alia.

At the secondary school, teachers have developed emergency plans for settler attacks and incorporated lessons on avoiding confrontations into their curriculum, trying to preserve a sense of normality for their students.

“The school’s aim is that when the children enter the school, and when they go home, they are protected,” said Bassam Abu Assaf, the 54-year-old principal of al-Mughayyir secondary school. “The amount of time we spend sitting is almost nonexistent. Our eyes are outside the school. We’re thinking, God forbid, there could be a settler attack against us.”

Despite the precautions, students’ educations have inevitably been disrupted. About 80% of the school staff live outside the village, and they are often prevented from entering the school by the Israeli military checkpoint. School is only in session for three days a week, and ends early so teachers don’t get caught by the road closure, which typically happens in the afternoon. Once, the Israeli army shot teargas near the school and the noxious fumes blew into the classrooms, with teachers powerless to stop it.
Related: The Palestinian school under siege – podcast

“Today there was news that settlers were present outside. Now, the student is sitting in front of you, but they’re not paying attention. He’s thinking about the danger that could come from the army, from the settlers. ‘Where are the settlers? Where is the army?’ That’s what he’s thinking about,” said Abu Naim, the teacher. His own brother was killed last April in a settler attack outside the school.
“You try as much as possible to make the student concentrate with you – but the educational gap becomes very large because of the number of days when the student can’t concentrate,” he said.
Abu Assaf, who attended the school he now heads, remembers a different childhood in the village, when children could roam freely through the surrounding hills.
“We could walk around, coming and going. Everything was open. We’d have fun, we’d barbecue. Now, the kids are stuck in their homes, seeing the world through their phones,” he said.
At noon the bell rang, marking the end of the school day. Students gathered in the yard as teachers peered over the gates to see if any settlers were about. Seeing none, they let the students out.
“There is a plan of displacement. But we will raise another educated generation regardless. Our aim is to confront these attacks through education,” said Abu Naim.

articles.title: Denmark pushes for EU ban on ‘turbo chickens’ as secret footage causes outrage
articles.summary: Minister says government will work towards banning fast-growing breed across country and throughout EU
body: The Danish government is pursuing a national ban on “turbo chickens” and is calling for the fast-growing breed to be prohibited across Europe.
The move comes amid widespread outrage over allegations of lawbreaking by one of Denmark’s big chicken producers.

According to a TV2 documentary broadcast last week, producer Christian Tvergaard broke Danish law by giving chickens only half the amount of darkness a day that is required, in order to encourage them to eat more. The documentary featured secretly filmed footage from a chicken coop in North Jutland.

The Ross 308 breed, labelled the turbo chicken, is the most widespread in Danish poultry production. It grows from about 50 grams to 2kg in just 33 days. Such rapid growth can lead to problems with the animal’s bones and organs. Other chicken breeds take between 46 and 63 days to reach the same weight.

Denmark’s minister for nature and animal welfare, Christian Rabjerg Madsen, said he discouraged Danes from buying turbo chickens, telling the broadcaster: “I want to work for a national ban. But it’s clear that this is something that needs to be investigated both legally and economically.” He added: “Now we will work for a national ban, we will work for a ban at EU level.”

In response to the documentary, Tvergaard has admitted to making some wrong decisions. He told TV2: “I look inward and must admit that I have made some wrong decisions. There is no excuse for that, but I can learn from it and correct where I have not done well enough.
“And I have done that, both when it comes to the lighting programme and a number of the workflows we have in the stable, where both procedures and the roster have been tightened up.”

The proposal for the ban on turbo chickens is gaining political momentum and attracting cross-party support in Denmark. But industry figures warn that to be effective, any ban must include imported chickens as well.

Klement Hinkbøl Ribergaard, the chief executive of chicken producer Danpo, said: “If Denmark alone bans the production of fast-growing chickens while shops, restaurants and consumers in the Danish market can continue to buy imported, fast-growing chicken of more or less questionable quality, we risk a situation in which animal welfare certainly does not benefit.”

With fast-growing breeds so prominent across the EU, it would mark a landmark shift. According to Eurogroup for Animals, 95% of chickens in the bloc are now raised in intensive systems and bred to produce the cheapest amount of meat possible, creating a “race to the bottom”.

“Fast-growing breeds are inherently predisposed to suffering, with their bodies growing so quickly they can barely stand on their legs,” said Reineke Hameleers, the advocacy group’s chief executive. “Denmark’s political willingness to stop this is an example that should be followed by the EU, for it presents the progressiveness this industry needs, one that is backed up by scientific evidence.”

Britta Riis, chief executive of Animal Protection Denmark, said turbo chickens were the result of a “deeply unethical and grotesque form of breeding” that led to “systematic abuse” and considerable suffering for the birds. The organisation is calling for all chickens to be bred for the same amount of time as organic breeds, which is 56 days.

Animal welfare has featured heavily in public debate in recent months in Denmark. The issue of pig farming dominated the last general election to such an extent that it was nicknamed the “pig election”.
The country is due to stop mink farming by August 2029 after the current government decided not to seek an EU exemption on the practice.

articles.title: PM to ask countries affected by UK’s role in slavery to help shape formal apology
articles.summary: Andy Burnham to launch ‘structured dialogue’ on issue at Commonwealth summit in Antigua and Barbuda
body: Andy Burnham will ask countries affected by Britain’s role in slavery to help shape an expected formal apology, Downing Street has indicated, arguing that their input is indispensable in crafting an enduring message.

The prime minister was en route to the Commonwealth heads of government summit (Chogm) in Antigua and Barbuda, which begins on Tuesday. No 10 said he would use the event to launch a “structured dialogue” into what form an apology might take.
UK officials already at the summit said other Commonwealth countries had responded positively to the move, and that it could help talks on separate issues such as trade and the climate.
In comments released by No 10 before Burnham’s arrival, the prime minister said discussion of an apology marked a new approach towards the UK’s relations with the Commonwealth.

Downing Street has ruled out the idea of paying reparations after an apology, but Burnham is expected to set out plans at the summit for a system of debt restructuring for countries facing higher debt costs.

“In today’s more divided, unpredictable world, the Commonwealth has the potential to be a powerful force for good, bringing together a third of the global population, and I believe it is key that the UK plays its full role in that,” Burnham said.“Britain is bringing a new approach to this meeting as we look to reshape a new era for the Commonwealth, as well as being open to discussions about the past.”

Burnham set out his intention to look at a possible apology in an article for the Guardian on Saturday, in which he said the UK should “show leadership again today” as it had done in efforts to end the transatlantic slave trade.

Asked why Burnham believed an apology was needed, his official spokesperson said: “The prime minister wants to strengthen the Commonwealth as a family of nations with shared values that can support growth around the world through trade and economic collaboration.” Having conversations about an apology would do this, and was also the right thing to do, he said.
Tony Blair expressed “deep sorrow” about the slave trade and Britain’s role in it in 2006, but stopped short of a formal apology.

Burnham intended to go further, his spokesperson said. “The prime minister, like his predecessors, has expressed his sorrow and regret for the pain and suffering caused by the transatlantic slave trade, and recognised the way it still shapes our world today.
Related: Monday briefing: The world is demanding reparations for enslavement – is Britain finally listening?

“That is distinct from a formal apology. We are opening a structured dialogue with those affected by the transatlantic slave trade, and listening to calls for a formal apology on behalf of the British state, and that will form an important part of that process.

“We think it’s right that a formal apology is discussed properly with the countries and communities most affected, rather than simply deciding unilaterally what form it should take. An apology of this significance should be informed by the people and countries most affected, as they have asked for.”
Burnham is scheduled to take part in a series of assemblies at Chogm, as well as bilateral meetings with other leaders.

There was no single event set aside to discuss slavery or an apology, but discussions would take place “throughout the next couple of days”, No 10 said, adding that the Foreign Office would lead talks over the form of an apology.

The foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, is already at the summit. One Foreign Office official said other Commonwealth countries “are responding positively to our offer of a structured dialogue” on an apology.

“The conversations at Chogm have been focused on the positive work this alliance can do together on issues like climate and trade,” they said. “By not shying away from difficult discussions about our past, we are building trust with our allies to focus on the big issues of the future.”
No 10 denied that Burnham’s comments had potentially embarrassed King Charles, who is already in Antigua and Barbuda for a pre-Chogm visit.

Buckingham Palace “was made aware in a timely manner”, Burnham’s spokesperson said. “The prime minister believes that being true to British values of decency and honesty means not shying away from these conversations.”

articles.title: How the EU can resist the divisive influence of the far right
articles.summary: Letters: Thomas Laffitte on the threats facing the European Union and Giorgio Re on why the strongest defence must come from the democratic right and centre-right
body: Your editorial rightly highlights the European far right’s maturing plans for Brussels’ political machinery (The Guardian view on the far right’s plans for Brussels: doing the work of Xi, Putin and Trump, 27 October). Alongside these developments, the evolution of Euroscepticism itself deserves closer attention.

As I argued in a recent report from the Brussels Institute for Geopolitics, anti-EU politics may have entered a phase of “post-Euroscepticism”. The discourse remains, but the ambition to dismantle the union has increasingly given way to blocking the march towards an ever closer union while retaining the existing structure and exploiting it.

Ten years after Brexit, this shift reflects a deeper change in the global geopolitical order. With the return of great-power politics and the rise of geoeconomic rivalries, even radical nationalists may be reluctant to part with the great instrument of power that the EU has become. Giorgia Meloni’s unexpectedly pragmatic approach to EU cooperation is a prime example.

The EU’s institutional architecture offers some resilience. Its weak centre and dispersion of authority make it comparatively difficult for any one government to capture the entire polity. Yet this strength is also a weakness. Institutional divisions can translate into misalignment, dysfunction and, ultimately, decay. The EU will endure, but escalating nationalist rivalries risk compounding this tendency for inertia and the irrelevance that results.

This makes the negotiations over the next multi-annual financial framework (2028–34) particularly important. The EU must strengthen its competitiveness and strategic autonomy, while preserving the cohesion funds that remain one of its greatest success stories. Peripheral regions, where Euroscepticism has gained considerable ground, must not be forgotten.

The danger facing Europe is no longer confined the prospect of its dismantlement. It also lies in the erosion of its capacity to act at a time when the return of geopolitics makes collective European power increasingly necessary. Thomas LaffitteResearch fellow, Brussels Institute for Geopolitics

• I felt compelled to write this letter after reading your editorial. I believe my feelings are shared by millions of Europeans whose voices are too often overlooked in today’s political debate – Europeans who value the freedom to live, study, work, do business and access healthcare across borders. And who believe that our common future deserves greater ambition.

As an Italian, coming from one of the six founding countries of European integration, and as a committed liberal conservative, I see no contradiction between defending individual freedoms, free enterprise, national identities and a stronger EU. Quite the opposite: in a world increasingly shaped by competing superpowers, European sovereignty can only be meaningfully exercised together.

However, defending Europe also requires acknowledging its shortcomings. Excessive bureaucracy, fragmented decision-making, sluggish economic growth and inadequate coordination on immigration and defence have contributed to public frustration. These deserve serious political answers rather than being dismissed as expressions of Euroscepticism.

That’s why I also believe that the strongest defence against nationalism must come from Europe’s democratic right and centre-right. We need European institutions that concentrate on what we can achieve better together: defence, external borders, strategic infrastructure, research and foreign policy. Mainstream conservative parties must resist the temptation to imitate nationalist rhetoric. They should instead articulate a confident, patriotic and genuinely pro-European alternative.

Some of Europe’s founding fathers, including Alcide De Gasperi, Konrad Adenauer and Robert Schuman, came from the Christian democratic tradition of the political centre-right. Their successors have a responsibility to carry that ambition forward.

I remain optimistic. Millions of centre-right Europeans believe in democracy, freedom and European unity. Their political voice could prove decisive in Europe’s future.Giorgio ReAgrigento, Sicily, Italy

articles.title: A diplomatic incident in Ealing over Kim Jong-un’s haircut

articles.title: Shop fridges and freezers across Europe hit by fresh suspected cyber-attack
articles.summary: Chains in seven countries say cooling unit temperatures rose overnight in incident similar to hack of French stores
body: Supermarket chains in at least seven European countries have said the temperatures of refrigerators and freezers in some of their shops soared overnight to as high as 50C (122F), echoing a cyber-attack last month that caused millions of euros of damage in France.

Retailers in Belgium, Estonia, Ireland, Finland, Luxembourg, the Netherlands and Sweden reported problems with their refrigeration systems on Monday, and several companies confirmed they had been hacked.

The EU food and agriculture commissioner, Christophe Hansen, said the repeated cyber-attacks were deeply concerning, calling them “a deliberate attempt to disrupt our food supply chain and undermine consumers’ confidence in it”.

The incidents follow an attack in France last month in which hackers seized control of cooling units in as many as 700 supermarkets, raising their temperatures as high ⁠as 50C (122F) and causing fires and food losses estimated in the tens of millions of euros.

A growing range of devices, including refrigeration systems, can now be monitored and controlled remotely, leading authorities to particularly fear government-sponsored hybrid attacks ​in after Russia’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine.

Sweden’s Coop chain told the daily Aftonbladet that six of ​its shops ‌had been ​hit, while ICA said it was “aware that a limited ​number of stores were affected by an incident overnight which impacted their refrigeration and freezer systems”.

An ICA shop at Sjöbo in southern Sweden posted that its fridges and freezers had been hacked and their temperature set at 50C. Another in Stockholm said its freezers were broken “due to a 2am cyberattack” and that “everything was destroyed”.

The head of Sweden’s national cybersecurity centre, John Billow, said it ‌was working on incidents around the country. It had established the country had “quite a lot of exposed operational ‌technology devices” that needed updating or patching, he told Reuters.

The Dutch retailer Ahold Delhaize, which last ​month ​reported a ​similar incident ​to police in the Netherlands, said fridges and ⁠freezers in dozens of its ⁠supermarkets in ​Belgium ‌and ‌Luxembourg had been hit.

It did not specify the cause, but reporters visiting a shop north-east of Brussels saw refrigerators and freezers empty and a sign reading: “Due to cyberattacks, there will be no products on the refrigerated or freezer shelves. We offer our sincere apologies.”

A company spokesperson, Sarah ‌De Meester, said the range of fresh and frozen products was “temporarily somewhat limited” in affected shops, but that distribution centres were operating normally and there was no disruption to deliveries.

Belgium’s Le Soir newspaper reported that dozens of shops and supermarkets had been affected, including five Spar outlets, Shop & Go convenience shops attached to Q8 service stations and some smaller Proxy Delhaize mini-markets.

“We started mobilising technicians at 1am,” Stephan Moelans, the chief executive of Sabcobel, which operates Delhaize’s refrigeration systems, told the paper. “We spent all night and morning disconnecting the affected installations.”
He told the Belga news agency the ‌incident had been a cyber-attack and that the units’ evaporators were switched to defrost mode.

The Colruyt and Intermarché supermarket chains also said they had been hit by technical problems affecting fridges in five and 15 of their shops respectively, and Carrefour Belgium reported disruption in about 15 of its 700 shops.
Related: Not cool: who hacked France’s supermarket fridges?

“It’s a cyber-attack, there is no other reason,” said Mich Vergauwen, a Carrefour spokesperson. An Ikea Belgium spokesperson likewise told Agence France-Presse that a cyber-attack had caused the temperature of freezers in its Mons shop to rise suddenly.
Ikea, famous for its in-store Swedish meatballs, said it had had to ‌remove some food products from refrigeration units ​as a precaution and expected some food waste as ⁠a result.

In Finland, the Helsingin Sanomat newspaper said shops operated by the Kesko supermarket chain were investigating similar problems, while the Dutch public radio NOS reported that the systems of at least 17 mainly small local shops had been affected.

At one Estonian supermarket chain, attackers accessed a computer controlling the refrigeration system and turned up the temperature to 50C, the refrigeration supply company Kitman Coldtech told the ERR broadcaster.

“This is very fresh, it happened this morning,” its chief executive, Jann Mutso, said, adding that the attack was responded to within minutes and there had been no significant damage. The Selver supermarket chain said one of its outlets had been affected.

Ireland’s third-largest supermarket ⁠chain, ⁠SuperValu, said ​refrigeration systems limited ⁠to ​a ‌specific ‌model ‌in 13 of its 223 shops ‌had been affected by ​a cyber-incident, ⁠and that chilled and ​frozen products ​had been removed from ​sale.

Many cyber-attacks involve extortion or are politically motivated and are potentially carried out by state-level actors, said Tom Hegel of the cybersecurity firm SentinelOne. But the supermarket attacks, with no financial demands, point to sabotage, he said.
“Retail is an easy target because retail chains run enormous estates of refrigeration controllers, building management systems, door access panels and point-of-sale gear,” Hegel told Reuters.

Patrick Lamplmair of the cybersecurity firm Tributech said cyber-attackers would keep going “until it stops working” because the method was “cheap and the damage is immediate”. Many refrigeration systems had known and as yet unfixed flaws, he said.
“Thousands of these controllers were still reachable from the internet after the French attack,” he added. “A few commands to a temperature controller can destroy stock overnight and close stores.”

In the French attack, the hackers pirated controllers mostly supplied by the Danish company Danfoss, which said subsequently that it had identified some security flaws last year and had “long recommended” customers install updates.

The hackers remotely overrode the settings on thousands of freezers, fridges and chiller cabinets at chains including Intermarché, Coopérative U, Carrefour, Leclerc and Monoprix, pushing them from as low as -27C to well over 50C.

The shops had to discard vast quantities of fresh meat, dairy and frozen products. Individual supermarkets reportedly suffered losses ranging from tens of thousands of euros to more than €130,000 (£109,000).

The Paris prosecutor’s office has opened a formal investigation into the French attack and the prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, instructed France’s national cybersecurity agency, Ansii, to investigate.

The agency subsequently reported that supermarkets using controllers from two other companies had also been targeted in the attack, but authorities have not indicated who could have been behind the incidents. There have been no claims of responsibility.

articles.title: Hackers send fake nuclear threat alert to Ukraine emergency app
articles.summary: Residents in Kyiv also warned of chemical attack and street-to-street fighting in false message sent by unknown party
body: Unknown hackers have targeted Ukraine’s nationwide emergency alert mobile app, sending residents in Kyiv a warning that they were at risk of an imminent nuclear strike.

The app reported a high possibility of nuclear radiation late on Sunday. It also wrongly warned of a chemical threat to the Ukrainian capital and street-to-street fighting. The messages were written in English with spelling mistakes, as well as in Ukrainian.

Many residents ignored the alerts, which began shortly before 11pm local time, assuming that the app had been compromised. Others were scared. “I was briefly terrified,” one woman, Nina, said. “I lay on my bed and wondered what was coming.”

A message written in Russian also claimed Ukraine was about to be hit by Oreshnik missiles, which can carry nuclear warheads. The Kremlin has used the ballistic weapon three times before, hitting the Kyiv region and the cities of Dnipro and Lviv.

In a post on Sunday, the Ukrainian emergency app said “unauthorised parties” had interfered with its operation. The channel had been temporarily suspended, it said, warning users not to click on links in “suspicious notifications”.

It was unclear on Monday who might have carried out the cyber-raid, or why. Russian officials claimed hackers had also sent fake emergency alerts there after gaining access to the app of the ministry for emergencies, based in Moscow.

One of their posts mentioned the hacking group Hitcore. Mash, a Russian Telegram channel with links to the security services, said it had spoken to representatives of Hitcore and that they had claimed responsibility for the attack. The report could not be verified.

The fake nuclear threats to Ukraine came as Russia resumed its attacks on the southern city of Kherson, hours after the end of a ceasefire during which hundreds of people were evacuated from the nearby Kremlin-controlled town of Oleshky.

Kherson’s military administration said a Russian drone hit a hospital at 7.40am. Video footage showed wrecked rooms, with windows blown out, doors broken, and debris on the street. Nobody was hurt, officials said.

There is evidence that the Russian army used the six-day ceasefire, which the White House said was brokered by the first lady, Melania Trump, to strengthen its positions in Oleskhy and to rotate in new troops. Bodies of dead civilians were also removed from a hospital morgue.

Footage shared with Sky News showed Russian soldiers deploying heavy military equipment and delivering ammunition. They carried large bags into burnt-out houses and buildings and disappeared into basements, the broadcaster reported.

Armoured vehicles were spotted moving around Oleshky’s streets. The occupied city is 3 miles from Kherson, on the opposite bank of the Dnipro River. Before last week’s truce, resupply was difficult because of the threat from Ukrainian kamikaze drones.
Related: Ukraine defies Trump to resume attacks on Russian oil refineries

According to the commander of Ukraine’s 34th Separate Marine Brigade, Dmitry Pulinets, Russian soldiers were previously unable to drive in the city, “neither during the day, nor at night, nor in bad weather”.
“Now they have this opportunity. And for the last few days this movement has been happening constantly,” he told Sky News.

The ceasefire expired at 11pm on Sunday. Both sides hailed the local pause in the fighting – the most significant since 2022 – as a success. Ukraine’s ombudsman, Dmytro Lubinets, who visited Oleshky to coordinate the mission, said it could be repeated in other occupied cities in the Kherson region.

He declined to say how many Oleskhy residents had chosen to go to Ukraine and how many to Russia, citing an agreement with Moscow to keep the figure secret. Ukrainian media have reported that most of the evacuation buses headed to Ukraine through Crimea, from where a plane took them to Gomel, a city in Belarus. Melania Trump said in a post that more than 750 people had left.

Lubinets paid tribute to the US first lady and said he had been in daily contact with her via her aide Marc Beckman. He said he hoped to bring back some of the “thousands of people” who had disappeared, as well as prisoners of war and bodies retrieved last week from Oleshky’s morgue. There were millions of Ukrainian citizens living in occupied territory, he said.

Vladimir Putin’s spokesperson Dmitry Peskov, however, said on Monday that there were no immediate plans for another truce elsewhere. He said it was standard practice for army units to regroup in such circumstances and that he assumed Ukraine’s armed forces had done the same.

Meanwhile, officials in the western region of Vinnytsia said two civilians had been killed in a drone strike next to an education facility. The victims were a 13-year-old girl, who died at the scene from her injuries, and a woman, who died later in hospital. Several other children were wounded, the officials said.

articles.title: ‘Traitors in every family’: Hungary to unmask communist-era informants and confront past
articles.summary: From 1945 to 1989 security police relied on tens of thousands of spies to suppress dissent. To rebuild trust, their files will finally be made public
body: Hungary’s new government will on Wednesday reveal the names of tens of thousands of state informants from the communist era in an attempt to confront the past and rebuild public trust.

From 1945 to 1989, Hungary’s communist state-security services relied on an extensive network of informants to monitor society and suppress dissent. Some were blackmailed or coerced into reporting on neighbours, friends, colleagues and even family members; others were recruited through promises of various advantages.

For decades, the extent of this network was hidden from public view. The “agent files”, held in the basement of the Historical Archives of the State Security services, remained largely inaccessible to the public, despite repeated calls and partial leaks.
During his campaign leading up to Hungary’s April parliamentary elections, Péter Magyar promised to make the state-security files public, a promise he seems intent on fulfilling now he is in power.

In September, his government passed a law paving the way for the files to be made public, a move more than two-thirds of the country supported according to polls. The release was initially scheduled for the anniversary of the 1956 anti-Soviet revolution but was pushed back to 4 November.
“A democratic society has the right to know its past,” Zoltán Tarr, the minister of social relations and culture, wrote on Facebook.

Previously, access to the reports on informants was restricted to researchers and relatives of victims. With the new, searchable online database, Hungary’s former state-service will become the most transparent in the former eastern bloc, researchers say.
“We are opening wide a door that was left ajar,” said István Papp, a historian and head of the academic department of the archives.
Related: Soviet troops invade Hungary – archive, 1956

“As a historian, I agree with the release of the files. But on a personal level, I feel for those who will face their family’s history for the first time,” Papp said. Of the 50,000 to 60,000 people whose names appear in the files, historians estimate 10% are alive today.

For three decades, the former eastern bloc has been divided on how to publish agent files, and when. In East Germany, the Bundestag opened state security Stasi files in 1992. In the Czech Republic, they became open to the public in 2003. Most recently, Latvia published files on informants in 2018.

Miklós Kiss, a survivor of a Hungarian forced labour camp and president of an association for victims, would have preferred if Hungary had followed Germany’s example and released the files earlier. “If that would have happened, everything would be done and dusted by now.
“People will learn that there were traitors in every family, in every neighbourhood and street,” he added. “But what are we supposed to do with that now?”

Placed side by side, the documents would stretch for three miles, enough to trace the perimeter of London’s Hyde Park. Even so, the collection is small compared with that of the Polish or Romanian secret services, Papp said. In Hungary, many files were destroyed during the 1956 anti-Soviet uprising; others disappeared during the transition of 1989, a gradual, largely peaceful process that gave the authorities time to get rid of incriminating material.
